story_text.value:
Openai just launched their decisions endpoint, cloudflare launched clef the other week, and many more jev alternatives are out there.

We wanted to put the popular ones to the test and thought Pac-Man is a good benchmark for simple and fast decision making.

So we let jev 1.13, kev, clef, clef flash, GPT-6 Luna and Laya play Pac-Man against bot ghosts.

The low latency of these models allows for real time play. We had each model play 100 games, published a leader board and open-sourced the repo so anyone can run their own model and join the ranking. Link to repo: https://github.com/opper-ai/jevman-benchmark/blob/main/CONTR...

You can also join the game and play as Pac-Man yourself, and the ghosts are the models, either a mix of models or all jev, kev, clef etc. A game costs about 2 cent, all models are running via my startup opper, and we added free credits for everyone to try.

It's pretty fun to play and surprisingly difficult to beat jev's highscore. Any feedback is more than welcome!

story_text.value:
[Abyss](https://abyss.scurry.io/) is my take on a local-first agent containerization framework for ACP agents. It aims to neatly solve 2 issues:

1. Agents having full access to your desktop, and thus indiscriminate access to your files/secrets/etc.

2. Agent/harness features having to be re-implemented for each agent, even if the feature isn't tied to the specific agent in any way.

The former is largely self-explanatory, I think. I want to log into my bank, I don't want my agent to even have the ability. There's a fair bit of software in this space already. I'll loop back to the advantages of Abyss' containerization vs others in a second, but the 30,000 foot overview is that Abyss runs your agent in a Docker container and proxies the ACP connection so it works with Zed/Openclaw/whatever.

The second is the more interesting and novel (as far as I'm aware). The current zeitgeist is heavily agent-specific, even for features that only read/manipulate the context (which isn't agent-specific). If you want RAG, you're writing an agent-specific plugin. If you want subagents, you're writing an agent-specific plugin even though a subsession is really just context. As a user, that can leave you tied to a particular agent just so your plugins continue to work.

Abyss solves that by taking a page from Nginx's book. Abyss supports WASM-based plugins that have full access to read and manipulate ACP messages flowing back and forth. Plugins can hide secrets in prompts from users before the agent ever sees them, implicitly hydrate prompts with RAG, inject MCP servers and more. There's a diagram showing what the flow of messages look like [in the docs](https://abyss.scurry.io/docs/guides/04-plugins/02-developing...), and there's a sample plugin [in the repo](https://github.com/SethCurry/abyss/tree/main/plugins/secrets...) that will auto-cancel a session if the agent outputs an OpenRouter API key in tool calls and responses (sample screenshot [on this page](https://abyss.scurry.io/docs/guides/what-is-abyss/#i-am-not-...)).

Plugins currently only run on the host, mostly because I haven't written something to install/distribute them inside the containers that's better than an 8GB Docker image or forcing users to make a custom Docker image.

Current Features:

- Fully agent-agnostic: pre-build images exist for Pi, Hermes, Claude and Codex but it works with any agent that supports ACP

- Supports both bind-mounting host directories and having Abyss copy files in on startup (so the agent can see them but can't change your copy)

    - Includes pathing support to mount them at the same path as on the host so your `@file.md` references still work
- Supports startup scripts, so you can add Node/Go/Rust/etc to your agent container without having to write a Dockerfile

- Manages the full Docker lifecycle; point Zed at Abyss and Abyss handles creating/stopping containers, mounting directories, etc

- Agent containers can be ephemeral or persistent

    - Persistent containers leave the agent running; running Abyss will re-connect to a running container (or create one if it doesn't exist)

    - Ephemeral containers are created and then torn down every time you invoke Abyss, giving you a consistent environment for batch-type jobs
- WASM plugins allow creating functionality reusable across agents

- Connections between your editor and the agent are encrypted and use mutual TLS for authentication

    - Certificates are ephemeral, and each container gets its own certs (they are single-use for ephemeral containers)
Future Wishlist:

- Backends other than Docker (most of this isn't Docker-specific, just a first target) - Remote backends (requires figuring out how to make something bind-mount-ish work on remote hosts)

Feedback, feature requests and bug supports are welcome!

story_text.value:
I built glog for myself and other humans who still read code and use Git while coding agents do more of the writing.

In other Git TUIs, my muscle memory from `git log` and `git show` accidentally triggered destructive rebases. glog is strictly read-only, so I can browse without worry.

It shows commits with syntax highlighting via delta, uses familiar pager keys, and has opinionated, human-friendly defaults. Supports expanding and collapsing diff contents and many more.

story_text.value:
DCSS is a venerable open source roguelike. Seeded games are an opt-in variant and there's a small community around sharing "interesting" seeds or ones particularly suited to certain builds or playstyles.

This runs dcss's dungeon gen and dumps seed data via a patched lua script. It's not meant to be a full enumeration of seeds, nor a complete dump of any particular seed. Just a way to find some interesting ones. I have about 1.3m for the most recent major version and you can add any valid seed to the corpus.

And seeds are strictly PER VERSION so if you want to play one on webtiles make sure's it's serving one of the versions I have seeds for and not trunk.

It grew out of a tool I'd been dragging around for years and finally decided to put a web interface over.

OCaml, sqlite, htmx alright alright.

https://crawl.develz.org https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dungeon_Crawl_Stone_Soup

story_text.value:
Hi HN. CandleFeed is a small API for crypto derivatives data (funding, open interest, liquidations). We wanted to test execution ideas against what the Binance book looked like, and commercial tick data cost more than we could justify for one venue, so in June we started recording it.

Three nodes record USD-M depth@100ms diff stream, the trade stream, and a 1,000-level REST snapshot every 5 minutes. Two are in Tokyo on different providers and one is in Singapore. A nightly job merges them: an update from a second node only goes in where Binance's update-id chain (pu equals the previous u) stays continuous, and where nodes overlap, their copies have to match, or the day is held back. Anything all three missed goes into a public gap log. The largest trade gap so far: on 2026-08-19 at about 15:28 UTC, all three nodes lost the same 32,153 trades across ten symbols, about 4 to 5.5 seconds' worth depending on the symbol.

A surprise: on 2026-09-25, 848 of the 861 BTCUSDT snapshots our three nodes took landed partway through a diff event. (That count comes from the nodes' raw copies; the published snapshot file carries one node's snapshots.) Replay has to apply that "straddling" event in full, so we tag every snapshot clean, straddle or in_gap.

Try it without an account: `curl https://candlefeed.ai/api/v1/l2/sample` lists the two open days, BTCUSDT and DOTUSDT book data for 2026-10-01. In Python, after `pip install "candlefeed[l2]>=0.3.2"`, run `from candlefeed import CandleFeed` and then `CandleFeed(public=True).download_l2_sample("DOTUSDT", "2026-10-01", "data/")`. That downloads the DOT day (about 100 MB) and checks every file's SHA-256. Sample files, with or without an account, are for internal use under our Terms (https://candlefeed.ai/terms, §5.3), so please don't re-host them. With a free account, the 1st of each month is free for every symbol (10 GiB a month). Pro is $149/mo for the full archive.

Our MCP server, candlefeed-mcp (`pip install candlefeed-mcp`, https://pypi.org/project/candlefeed-mcp/), lets Claude Code or Cursor pull a day and rebuild the book from a prompt; it needs a free API key. There's also a notebook that does it in plain Python on the 2026-10-01 BTCUSDT sample. It uses a free API key too; for a no-account run, swap its download call for `download_l2_sample`: https://candlefeed.ai/examples/l2-free-sample-day/

What's weak: one venue, 25 symbols (10 with history from June 2026, 15 from late September), and we can't backfill what we didn't record. It's also the 100ms stream, not Binance's fastest.

story_text.value:
Hi HN. Hence is a modern twist on the classic logic grid puzzle (zebra puzzles, Einstein's riddle): all the deduction, but every clue is a picture instead of a sentence.

There's a 4x4 and a 6x6 every day, the same for everyone. Free, no signup, and progress lives in your browser.

A few things I cared about:

- Every puzzle can be solved by deduction alone, so you never have to guess. Each one is checked against a solver before it ships. The solver verifies every puzzle is solvable from the clues alone, then trims the clues down to the minimum each difficulty level needs. - Hints are there for when you aren't noticing something. They nudge you in the right direction without giving too much away. - The art is a core part of the experience. Everything is designed toy-like: chunky, bold, and simple, so it looks fun and reads clearly on a small phone screen. Each item needed to have a unique shape and color so you can recognize it at a glance, and you can easily know what group it belongs to. A lot of thought went into every one of those decisions, and you'd never notice most of them while playing. What you get is a game that just feels fun.

The thing I'm still tuning is the first two minutes. I'd love to hear whether the difficulty felt about right, did you find it fun, do you want to play again, and would you send your result to a friend to challenge them against your result? (when you send, they play against what you solved)

https://hencegame.com
